title: Chapter 57 – Through the Seam
html:
[Lin Clan – Old Hu]

Hu is carrying a baby when he learns the truth, and it is the baby that saves him from saying something stupid.

She is eight months old, and she weighs about as much as a sack of wet sand, and she has decided, with the unshakable firmness of the young, that his beard is a toy. One small fist is wound round a hank of it. The other is exploring his nose. Her mother, a thin sobbing woman from the lower farms, has thrust her into his arm at the top of the cellar stair with a single wild glance, and run back for her other child, and Hu, who has not held an infant in forty years, has found himself standing in the dark with a squalling armful and only one hand to hold it.

"Hush," he says. "Hush, hush. It is a ugly beard. I know. Stop pulling it."

She does not stop.

Below him, the cellar stair goes down into a great, vaulted, whitewashed room that he has been in a hundred times, to fetch wine, or to hide from it. It is the hall's winter store. There are casks along one wall, and sacks of millet, and ropes of dried onion hanging from the beams. It is not a large place. It was built to hold a clan's winter food, not a clan.

There are three hundred and seventy people in it.

He sees them in the light of the one hooded lantern: old women on stools, with their hands in their laps; children sitting in rows on the floor, quiet, with their eyes enormous; a long line of men and women along the walls, with bundles tied in cloth; the schoolmaster, in his patched gown, with a book open on his knee, reading aloud in a steady quiet voice from the Founder's Precepts, to no one in particular, to everyone. A woman is weeping, softly, in the far corner. Nobody tells her to stop.

Above them, through the ceiling, comes a long dull rumble. It is the sound of a great many feet. And under it, faint and shrill and endless, like a wire drawn through the stone, is the sound of someone screaming.

They are in the courtyard, he thinks. They have broken the wall. He thinks of the Heaven's Door, the month of the Patriarch's life that went into it, and of how long a month is to a boy, and how short a hundred breaths. He thinks of Wenshi, somewhere above, with a bad wrist and a good sword, and the thirty men who have chosen to stay. He thinks that he has never in his life been so afraid for people he did not particularly like.

The baby pulls his beard again. He lets her. It is, he decides, the most honest opinion anyone has offered him all night.

"Hu."

He turns.

* * *

The boy is standing at the foot of the stair, in the lantern's gold, with a coil of white rope over one shoulder.

He looks dreadful. He is gray to the lips. There is dried blood in the corner of one nostril and a long raw scar behind his ear, and when he walks he favors the left side, as a man favors an old wound. But his eyes are quite steady. They are as steady as a drawn line, with that thin pale ring of gold round the black, and they go, one by one, over the faces in the cellar, and he does not look away from any of them.

The pangolin is on his shoulder. She is smaller than Hu remembers. She is so dull in the scales that she looks coated in ash.

"I need you," says Jian.

"I am holding a baby."

"I know. I am sorry." He does not smile. "Give her to Aunt Meirong. I need your hands. Both of them. Or the one you have."

Hu looks down at the child. She has fallen asleep with her fist in his beard. After a moment he hands her, carefully, to a plump gray-haired woman who has appeared at his elbow, and detaches the small fingers one by one, and flexes his hand.

"What do you need?"

"You to see something. And not shout."

"I have given up shouting."

"You shouted in the granary."

"That was a recipe," says Hu, with dignity.

The boy almost smiles. It is a ghost of the thing, a flicker. Then it is gone, and he turns, and walks to the north wall of the cellar, where a great black cask sits on a stone cradle against the whitewash, with a thick rope of dried onions hanging above it. He puts his small hand flat against the wall.

"Pebble," he says.

* * *

It begins, as it always begins, with a sound.

It is not loud. It is a sort of thin, high, sweet trilling, a long rising scale like the call of a night bird. It goes on for a very long time. The pangolin has slid from his shoulder to the floor, and sits up on her hind legs, with her tiny hands raised and her eyes shut, and the whole of her round dull body is trembling like a leaf.

The air in front of her begins to glow.

Hu has seen a great many things in sixty-seven years. He has seen the Veiled Forge burn. He has seen a man split a crucible with his bare hand. He has seen the Sect's Elders walk through a wall of fire as though it were a curtain. He has never, in all his life, seen the wall of a cellar come open.

It opens like a mouth. It opens from the center outward, a long thin vertical line of green light, a hand's breadth wide, then two, then three. It hums. It breathes. A cold wet gust rolls out of it, smelling of black earth and rain, and the lantern gutters in the wind, and from somewhere in the crowd a child says, in a high clear voice: "Mama, there's a door in the wall."

Nobody speaks.

Hu stands where he is. His mouth has fallen open. His one good eye, the dark and clear one, is fixed on the green light with an expression of such naked, such utter, such helpless wonder that a woman in the front row of the crowd, seeing it, begins very quietly to cry.

A seam, he thinks. A living one.

It is the thing he has looked for his whole life. It is the gap in the weave. It is the line along which all things break, and all things might be mended, the thing he found in a thousand blades and could never find in the world, the one flaw that is also a door. He has felt it in metal, once or twice, in the heart of a crucible, in the white second before a sword came true. He has never seen it made.

"It is a Seamwalker's door," says Jian, quietly. "It opens into a place under the hill. It is safe. It is the safest place I know. There is air, and water, and a roof, and a garden." His voice shakes, a very little. "It is where I have been going, for the last four months, when I was not in the granary."

Hu does not turn his head. "A garden."

"The Orchard. It has been in the hill four hundred years. Pebble was born in it. My father knows. My mother knows. I could not tell you. Not because I did not trust you, but because Mu would ask, and you would not lie."

"No," says Hu, faintly. "I should not have."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be." The old man's voice is a dry whisper. He is still looking at the light. "It is the finest thing I have ever seen."

"It will cost her." The boy's eyes are on the pangolin, on the thin trembling line of her back. "Every door costs her a scale. I have not asked her to open this one. She offered. I do not know how many she has left." He swallows. "I need you to take the rope, Hu. And go through first. And tell them it is safe."

"Why me?"

"Because they will believe you." The boy looks at him, quite simply. "You are the one man on the hill who has never once pretended to be anything but what he is."

* * *

It takes forty minutes.

He remembers it afterward in pieces, like a dream: the rope, thick and white, running from a ring in the cellar wall through the open seam and out of sight; the long slow file of the old and the young, each with a hand on the line, stepping one by one through the green light with a little hitch of breath, like swimmers going into cold water. The schoolmaster, with his book under his arm. A very old woman, carried by two sons. A dozen small boys with stones in their pockets. A girl of nineteen, in white, with a baby, who stops at the edge of the light and looks at the boy and says nothing, and goes through.

He goes first. He had not expected to. He puts his one hand on the rope, and steps in, and the cold takes him.

It is like falling through a waterfall. It goes up his arm and into his chest, and for one dizzying second he is nowhere, and everything, a point in a long bright thread. Then there is moss under his boot, and the smell of wet leaves, and a high pearl-gray light, and he is standing in a place so impossible that for a long time he cannot speak.

A garden.

It is not a garden. It is a world. A great hollow in the heart of the hill, vaulted over by a roof of glimmering stone, with veins of silver running through it like rivers on a map. Beds of tall dark plants in rings of white pebbles. A pool, far off, shining like a plate of green glass. And everywhere, in the air, in the moss, in the cool and drifting mist, the thick sweet slow breath of something that has been alive for a very long time, and is glad.

He kneels. He does not mean to. His knees simply give. He puts his hand flat on the moss, and the moss is warm.

Heartroot, he thinks, for no reason at all, looking at a bed of silver-gray leaves. Fifty plants.

I knew it.

He laughs. It is a cracked, hoarse, incredulous sound, and it echoes off the ceiling. It is a very long time since he has laughed like that. He is still laughing when the first of the clan comes through the light, an old farmer with a stick, and stops, and looks round, and says in a quavering voice: "Is it the ancestors?"

"No," says Hu, wiping his eye. "It is the vegetable garden."

* * *

They are all through by the second hour. He counts them. He cannot help it. Three hundred and sixty-eight. They sit on the moss in clusters, in the mild green dark, with their bundles in their laps and the cold hush of the garden round them, talking in whispers. They do not seem afraid. They seem, rather, like people who have been woken in the night and carried, very gently, to a place they cannot quite believe.

A small gray-robed boy is going among them with a skin of water.

Hu watches him. He is thin, and stooped with weariness, and he goes from face to face with the same careful courtesy, a word to each, a touch on a shoulder, as a man might who has been doing it all his life. He stops by an old woman who has begun to weep. He kneels. He says something. She laughs, through the tears, and pats his cheek.

He is ten years old, Hu thinks, with a sort of slow, appalled tenderness. He is ten years old, and he has built a hundred-year garden under a hill, and slain nine men in a tunnel, and rescued a seamwalker from a dead girl, and tonight he is giving old women water.

"You knew," says a voice at his elbow.

It is Wenqing. The herbalist is standing at his shoulder, in his green gown, with a bundle of white linen in his arms. His face is the color of dough. There is a smear of someone's blood across his forehead. In the other hand, hanging loose, he holds a short curved knife, wiped clean. He is staring at the pool.

"I did not," says Hu. "I guessed. A little."

"I have grown frostbell for twenty years. I have begged the Pavilion for a sack of Heartroot. I have sat at the lower terrace in the frost and wept over a seedbed." Wenqing's voice is a thin level whisper. "And it was here. It was here the whole time."

"Yes."

"Under my feet."

"Under all our feet."

The herbalist laughs. It is a short, dreadful, silent sound, a laugh with no breath in it. He sits down on the moss, quite suddenly, with the linen in his lap, and puts his face in his hands. His shoulders shake.

"I am sorry," he says. "I am sorry. It is only that I am very tired. I have killed a woman. I have been awake for forty hours. And a ten-year-old boy has just shown me a place where the world is kind."

Hu sits down beside him. He puts his one arm round the man's thin shoulders, and does not say anything. After a while, the shaking stops.

"The boy," says Wenqing, into his hands. "Does he know what it costs?"

"I think," says Hu slowly, "he is the only one who does."

* * *

It is the old smith who first sees the thing on the terrace.

He has gone, as he always goes, to look at the work. He cannot help it. It is the habit of fifty years: to find the weakest joint in any structure, and put his thumb on it. He walks along the pool's edge, past the dim Wardens standing in their ring, vast and silent, with their small green lamps burning. He climbs the three black steps of the terrace. And there, in the middle of the broad dark floor, he finds a great round plate of black metal, as wide as a cartwheel, with a long clean crack running through it from rim to rim.

He stops.

He goes down on his knee. He puts out his hand and lays it on the cold dull metal, and his fingers, with the old unconscious skill of a lifetime, run along the line of the break. It is a beautiful break. It is a clean, sweet, deliberate thing, the kind of crack that a master puts into a sword to show where the soul is.

Coral Gate, he thinks.

His breath stops.

It is the script. It is the very script. Not a copy, not a cousin, not a student's pale imitation, but the thing itself, drawn by a hand that knew exactly what it was doing, in fine black lines too delicate to follow, and so intricate that his eye begins to ache. It is a lock. It is, he realizes, the other half of the book in his pocket: the Hundred Veins, the first volume, whose last page has been blank for forty years. He has the manual for the key. He has been carrying it, wrapped in oilcloth, against his heart, since the day the Forge fell.

And here is the keyhole.

It is under a pool, he thinks. Of course it is under a pool. The Sect of the Pool. The Well, the Rill. They were never looking for a vault. They were looking for this.

The lamp-light shivers. He lifts his head.

The boy is standing at the foot of the steps. He has come up very quietly, in the way of one who has long since learned not to make a noise, and he is looking at Hu with an expression Hu cannot read. It is neither guilty nor afraid. It is simply very still, like a stone in a stream.

"You see it," says Jian.

"I see it."

"He wants it."

"He has wanted it for sixty years." Hu rises, stiffly, with a hand on his knee. "It is the lock to a vault. The oldest one there is. It was made for the Founder of the Pool, and the Founder is dead, and his last disciple is dying in a cell, and Mu has spent his whole life learning how to turn a key he has never seen." His voice is a dry rasp. "He will come here. Now. Tonight. Through the seam. He cannot help it."

"I know."

"You know?"

"I am going to leave it open."

For a long moment the old man looks at him. He does not speak. He is looking, he realizes, at the gold ring round the child's eyes, at the thin set mouth, at the small hard line between the brows that is exactly, precisely, to the very hair, the line of a man who is about to do a thing that he has already decided, and will do, and has not yet forgiven himself for.

"You have a plan," says Hu.

"I have a count."

"What is the count?"

"Eleven Wardens. One reservoir. One lock." The boy's voice is quiet. "One seam, left open, at the end of a long straight rope. And one Pool-stage cultivator who thinks that I am a small, brave, clever child, and has never once in his life been afraid of what a garden can do."

"A garden."

"He drained it," says Jian. "Once. He took the whole of its Qi, in an hour, and put it in a pool. It was the best thing he could have done." A small cold smile moves, for a second, across the child's face. "I would like to give it back."

Hu stares at him. He feels, quite distinctly, the hair rise on the back of his neck.

He means to drown him, he thinks.

It is a terrible thought. It is also, he finds, a very good one. A pool, a lock, a drain. A man who has come a long way, with a key in his hand, to a door that he cannot help but open. A hill that has been waiting four hundred years. A garden full of old, patient, dormant things, and a boy at the center, with a roll of needles and a pale scaled creature at his heel, who has never once in four months been caught without a plan.

"Tell me what you need," says Hu.

"Two things."

"Name them."

"The first is the key." The boy's eyes are very bright. "You have the Canon. You have the first volume. I need to know how it turns. I need to know which direction, and what it costs. I need to know what happens to a man who stands at the door when it opens."

Hu draws the book from his coat. It is a thin thing, bound in bone, with a cover that has gone dark with the oil of his skin. He does not open it. He holds it between his palms, as a man holds a bird.

"It is not a key," he says. "I thought it was, for forty years. It is a method. It teaches a smith how to forge a blade that will fit a particular lock, if he knows the lock. It does not say which lock. That was the secret. The Sect kept the lock, and the Forge kept the method, and neither could use the other." His thumb moves on the cover. "And now the lock is here, and the method is in my hand, and I do not know whether to weep or to burn the thing."

"How is it turned?"

"By a blade of Pool-grade iron, forged on the night of a new moon, quenched in blood, and laid in the keyhole point first." The old man's voice is flat. "The lock is a hand. It wants a palm. It will take the palm of anyone who stands at it, and read his blood, and decide whether he is the gardener. If he is not, it kills him." He pauses. "If he is, it opens."

"And Mu has the blade?"

"Mu has been forging it for eleven years. He needed only the seam." Hu looks at the crack in the plate. "And you have cracked it, boy. That is the part I do not understand. It is not meant to crack. It is meant to turn."

"It lifted a quarter inch," says Jian. "And stopped. I think it was waiting."

"For what?"

"For the Orchard to be full again." The boy's eyes are on the black metal. "It will not open to a thief. It will not open to a man with a key and a stolen garden. It wants a gardener, and a full pool, and a seam that has been asked, not forced." He turns his head. "That is what I think. I do not know it. But it is the only reason he would drain the place first."

A lock that opens only for a gift, thinks Hu.

It is a very old idea. It is the best idea in the world, and the Sect of the Pool, which has never given anything in its life, would not have understood a word of it.

"Then he cannot open it," he says slowly.

"No. Not alone." The boy's voice drops. "But he does not know that. And a man who thinks he can will try."

Behind them, a small sound. Hu looks round. Qinghe is standing at the edge of the terrace, with her hair down and a bloodstained sleeve, and a short thin knife in each hand, and her eyes on her son. She has come through last, after the guards, with the Patriarch's last word on her lips. She is very pale. She does not say anything at all.

"Mother," says Jian.

"I have left your father in the hall," says Qinghe. Her voice is perfectly level. "With Wenshi, and thirty men, and a very good sword. He says that he will hold the great stair for as long as the stair holds, and that you are not to be a hero." A small pause. "I told him that you were your father's son, and that it was a great deal too late."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be sorry. Be quick."

She crosses the terrace. She does not embrace him. She takes his face in both hands, hard, and looks into it for a long time, and kisses his forehead, once, and lets him go.

"Go," she says.

He goes.

* * *

"And the second?" says Hu.

"The second," says Jian, "is that you do not let anyone follow me."

Hu opens his mouth. He closes it. Somewhere, far above them, through two hundred feet of stone, a long dull sound comes down, as of a great door being slowly forced.

"I will not promise that," says the old man.

"No." The boy smiles, a very little. "I did not think you would."

He turns. He goes down the steps, and across the moss, and into the green dark, with a small pale thing trotting at his heel, and the old smith stands on the terrace with his one arm hanging and the Hundred Veins against his heart, and listens to the hill come down.
